usage: 부엌 takes 에서 because cooking is a dynamic action done there
describing the room itself uses 이/가 + descriptive verb
common chore collocation; 치우다 = clear away/tidy
살림 = household goods & housekeeping; a very natural pairing
examples: 부엌이 어디예요?
Where is the kitchen?
Simplest form: noun + 이 + 어디예요? to ask location
엄마가 부엌에서 김치찌개를 끓여요.
Mom is making kimchi stew in the kitchen.
Everyday scene: 에서 for the action + 을/를 for what she cooks
이사 온 집은 부엌이 좁아서 조금 불편해요.
The place we moved into has a small kitchen, so it's a bit inconvenient.
Real-life complaint: 부엌이 좁아서 (cause) leads into a reaction
nuance: 부엌 is the warm, native-Korean everyday word for the room where you cook and wash dishes — the heart of the home where the smell of food lives. Its nearest synonym is the Sino-Korean 주방 (廚房, 'cooking-room'): 주방 is the neutral, technical label you see on apartment floor plans, restaurant signs, and in compounds like 주방용품 (kitchen goods), whereas 부엌 carries a homier, more personal feeling — 우리 집 부엌 sounds natural, 우리 집 주방 sounds like a brochure. Both are everyday and polite; there's no status caution. It collocates with 요리하다, 치우다, and 부엌 살림. The classic English-speaker pitfall is the final consonant: it ends in ㅋ (부엌), so the spelling is fixed even though it's pronounced [부억] before a pause — never write 부억. The second trap is particle choice: use 부엌에서 for an action happening there, but 부엌에 for where something simply sits (부엌에 냉장고가 있어요).

The classic English-speaker pitfall is the final consonant: it ends in ㅋ (부엌), so the spelling is fixed even though it's pronounced [부억] before a pause — never write 부억. mistakes: Writing 부억 instead of 부엌 — it is pronounced [부억] before a pause, but the correct final letter is always ㅋ, so the spelling never changes.
Saying 부엌에 요리해요 for the action of cooking — an action done in a place needs 에서, so it must be 부엌에서 요리해요; 에 only marks where something exists.
Calling a restaurant or floor-plan kitchen 부엌 in a formal label — there the neutral word 주방 (주방용품, 공용 주방) is expected; 부엌 sounds like a cozy home kitchen.

usage: 에서 for the washing action; 욕실 stresses the bathing space
noun + noun compound; a routine chore phrase
(a room) comes with an attached bathroom
딸려 있다 = be attached/come with; real-estate vocabulary
욕실 + 수건; the towel kept in the bathroom
examples: 욕실이 깨끗해요.
The bathroom is clean.
Simple description: 이 + adjective 깨끗하다
아침마다 욕실에서 머리를 감아요.
Every morning I wash my hair in the bathroom.
Everyday routine: 에서 for the action; 머리를 감다 = wash one's hair
이 방에는 욕실이 따로 있어서 정말 편해요.
This room has its own separate bathroom, so it's really convenient.
Real-life: 따로 있다 (exists separately) + cause 어서
nuance: 욕실 (浴室, 'bathing-room') is the Sino-Korean word for the home room you wash and shower in, the part with the tub, sink, and showerhead. Its constant point of confusion is 화장실 (化粧室, literally 'makeup-room'): 화장실 foregrounds the toilet and is the word you actually say when you need to 'go to the restroom' or ask for one in public, while 욕실 foregrounds the bathing function of a private home. In most Korean homes these are physically the same room, so a guest asks 화장실 어디예요?, not 욕실 어디예요?. Both are polite and neutral. It collocates with 샤워하다, 욕실 청소, and the real-estate phrase 욕실이 딸려 있다. The English-speaker pitfall is treating 'bathroom' as one-to-one with 욕실: because English 'bathroom' usually means the toilet, learners over-use 욕실 in public settings where Koreans say 화장실. A second trap is the look-alike 거실 (living room) — 욕실 vs 거실 differ by just one syllable.

usage: read a book in the study
에서 for the action; the room's core use is reading
noun + noun shows whose private room it is
the study is full of books
가득하다 = be full; the typical look of a 서재
examples: 서재에 책이 많아요.
There are many books in the study.
Simple existence: 에 + 많다 for what's in the room
아빠는 저녁마다 서재에서 책을 읽어요.
Dad reads books in the study every evening.
Everyday habit: 에서 for the action + 마다 (every)
재택근무를 하면서 작은 방을 서재로 꾸몄어요.
While working from home, I turned the small room into a study.
Real-life: 으로 꾸미다 = arrange (something) into; 으로 marks the result
nuance: 서재 (書齋, 書 'book/writing' + 齋 'studio/room') is a private room inside a home set aside for reading, studying, and desk work, usually lined with bookshelves and quietly personal in feel — historically the scholar's room. Two synonyms get confused with it. 도서관 (圖書館, 'library') is a public building where anyone borrows books, the opposite of private; 교실 (敎室, 'classroom') is where a class is taught at school. 서재 is none of these — it is your own room at home. It is neutral and polite, often introduced by whose it is (아빠 서재, 할아버지 서재). It collocates with 책을 읽다, 책이 가득하다, and 서재를 꾸미다. The English-speaker pitfall is mapping 'study' onto 공부 (the activity of studying): 서재 is the physical room, never the act, so 'I have to study' is 공부해야 해요, not anything with 서재. A second pitfall is reaching for 서재 to mean a public library — that is 도서관.

Saying 서재해요 to mean 'I study' — 서재 is a room, not an action; the verb 'to study' is 공부하다 (공부해요).
Using 에 for the action of reading (서재에 책을 읽어요) — reading is done there, so it needs 에서: 서재에서 책을 읽어요. Use 에 only for where things are (서재에 있어요).

usage: 에 + 있다 for location below ground
지하 + number + 층; the standard way to count down-floors
지하 + noun compound; very common in apartments
examples: 마트는 지하에 있어요.
The supermarket is in the basement.
Simple location: 에 + 있다
지하 1층에서 주차하고 엘리베이터를 타요.
I park on B1 and take the elevator.
Everyday: 에서 for the action of parking; 지하 1층 = B1
이 건물은 지하 3층까지 주차장이 있어요.
This building has parking all the way down to B3.
Real-life: 까지 = up to/down to; counting multiple down-floors
nuance: 지하 (地下, 地 'earth/ground' + 下 'below') literally means 'below the ground' and covers both a home's basement and the underground levels of any building. Its exact antonym is 지상 (地上, 'above ground'); together they split a building, and the boundary syllable 지 is shared, so keep 지하/지상 straight by the 下(below)/上(above) ending. A near-synonym for a home cellar is 지하실 (地下室, the basement room itself): 지하 names the underground zone or floor, while 지하실 names a specific room — say 지하실에서 빨래해요 for the laundry room, but 지하 2층 for floor B2. 지하 is neutral and everyday. It collocates with 지하 주차장, 지하 1층, and 지하철 (the 'underground-iron-road,' i.e. subway). The English-speaker pitfall is floor order: floors going down are 지하 + number + 층 (지하 1층 = B1), with 지하 first — never 1층 지하. A second trap is using 'basement' for any low floor; 1층 (the ground floor) is above ground, not 지하.

Calling the ground floor 지하 — 1층 is above ground (지상); 지하 begins at 지하 1층, one level below the entrance floor.

usage: 에서 for an activity done up there
store things away in the attic
넣어 두다 = put away and leave; attics are for storage
아늑하다 = snug/cozy, the feeling a 다락방 evokes
examples: 다락방이 좀 더워요.
The attic is a bit hot.
Simple description: 이 + adjective; attics trap heat under the roof
아이들이 다락방에서 숨바꼭질을 해요.
The kids are playing hide-and-seek in the attic.
Everyday scene: 에서 for the activity + a child's game
안 쓰는 짐은 전부 다락방에 올려놨어요.
I put all the unused stuff up in the attic.
Real-life: 올려놓다 = put up and leave; 에 marks the destination
nuance: 다락방 is the small, cozy room tucked directly under the sloped roof, with a low ceiling — the kind of hideaway kids love and families fill with seasonal boxes and old keepsakes. It's a native Korean compound: 다락 (the loft space under a roof) + 방 (room), so 다락방 specifically stresses that the loft is a usable room, while plain 다락 names the storage loft as a space (다락에 넣다 = stash it in the loft). It is warm and everyday, never formal, and pairs with 올라가다, 아늑하다, and storage verbs like 넣어 두다 / 올려놓다. The clearest English-speaker pitfall is direction particles: when you go up to it, the goal takes 에 (다락방에 올라가요), but the activity done inside takes 에서 (다락방에서 놀아요) — English 'in the attic' hides this split. A second trap is confusing the up/down spaces: 다락방 is under the roof at the top, the opposite of 지하 (the basement below the house).

usage: 에 (destination) + 넣다 (put in); the core storage verb
쌓아 두다 = stack and leave; what storerooms fill with
가득 차다 = become packed full; 이/가 marks the subject
정리하다 = sort/tidy; a common weekend chore
examples: 창고가 너무 좁아요.
The storeroom is too small.
Simple description: 이/가 + adjective 좁다
겨울옷을 상자에 담아서 창고에 넣었어요.
I packed the winter clothes in boxes and put them in the storeroom.
Everyday: 에 + 넣다 for storing; 담아서 (pack and then) links the steps
창고에 짐이 너무 많아서 발 디딜 틈도 없어요.
There's so much stuff in the storeroom there's no room to even step.
Real-life idiom: 발 디딜 틈도 없다 = packed with no room to stand
nuance: 창고 (倉庫, 倉 'granary' + 庫 'storehouse') is any space for keeping things — it scales from a small home storeroom to an outdoor shed to a full industrial warehouse, so context sets the size. At home it's where boxes, tools, and off-season items live. Its dangerous look-alike and near-homophone is 차고 (車庫, garage): they differ by a single ㅇ batchim — 창고 (storage) vs 차고 (car-garage) — and even share the 庫(storehouse) hanja, so learners constantly swap them; remember 창고 has the extra ㅇ for 'th-ings,' while 차(car)고 holds a car. 창고 is neutral and everyday. It collocates with 넣다, 쌓아 두다, 정리하다, and 가득 차다. The key English-speaker pitfall is the particle with 넣다: putting something in takes the destination marker 에 (창고에 넣어요), not 에서 — 에서 would wrongly say the putting-action 'happens out of' the storeroom. A second pitfall is using 창고 for a car space; that specific meaning is 차고.

usage: put the car in the garage
에 (destination) + 넣다; the everyday way to say 'park inside'
주차하다 (park) is the more formal verb for the same act
차고 + 문 compound; the up-and-over door
back the car out of the garage
차를 빼다 = pull/take the car out; 에서 for the exit action
examples: 차고가 넓어요.
The garage is spacious.
Simple description: 이/가 + adjective 넓다
매일 밤 차를 차고에 넣어요.
Every night I put the car in the garage.
Everyday habit: 에 + 넣다 for parking it inside
차고에 차가 두 대나 들어가요.
The garage fits as many as two cars.
Real-life: counter 대 for vehicles + 나 ('as many as'); 들어가다 = fit in
nuance: 차고 (車庫, 車 'vehicle' + 庫 'storehouse', literally 'car-storehouse') is the home structure built to shelter a car, like a garage attached to a house. Two words sit close to it. The near-homophone 창고 (storeroom) differs by only an ㅇ batchim and shares the 庫 hanja, so they're endlessly mixed up: 차(car)고 holds a car, 창고 holds things. The functional near-synonym is 주차장 (駐車場, 'parking lot') — but that's the shared, often open lot for an apartment building or a public area, whereas 차고 is your own private, usually enclosed home garage; you'd say 아파트 주차장 but 우리 집 차고. 차고 is neutral and everyday. It collocates with 차를 넣다/빼다, 주차하다, and 차고 문. The English-speaker pitfall is particle direction with the same noun: parking in takes 에 (차고에 넣어요), but taking the car out takes 에서 (차고에서 빼요) — 에 is the goal, 에서 is the source. A second trap is using 차고 for an apartment's communal lot; that is 주차장.

usage: 에서 for the gardening action; 키우다 = raise/grow
가꾸다 = nurture and beautify; the signature verb for 정원
adjective 넓다 + noun; 정원 implies designed, planted space
examples: 정원이 예뻐요.
The garden is pretty.
Simple description: 이 + 예쁘다 (irregular ㅡ drops: 예뻐요)
주말마다 정원에서 잡초를 뽑아요.

nuance: 뒷마당 is the open yard behind a house — a casual, everyday space for kids, pets, chores, and weekend barbecues. nuance: 발코니 is a loanword (from English 'balcony') for an outdoor platform projecting from a room, fenced by a railing, where you can stand outside the building wall. 이/가 + adjective; describing the boundary wall

너머 = the far side past a barrier

Real-life: 사이에 (between) shows 담장 as a property boundary
nuance: 담장 is the outer wall or fence that encloses a house or its yard, marking the edge of the property — what you'd peek over to talk to a neighbor. Its plain synonym is 담, which means exactly the same boundary wall; 담장 just sounds slightly more substantial and concrete, and the two are freely interchangeable (담을 넘다 = 담장을 넘다). The crucial contrast is with 벽 (壁): 벽 is an interior or structural wall of a room or building (방 벽에 액자를 걸다, hang a frame on the room's wall), whereas 담/담장 is the outdoor perimeter wall — so a learner who says 담장에 그림을 걸어요 has hung a picture on the outside boundary wall, which sounds odd. 담장 is neutral and everyday. It collocates with 넘다, 쌓다, 높다, and 담장 너머. The English-speaker pitfall is that English 'wall' covers both indoor and outdoor: you must split it into 벽 (inside) vs 담/담장 (the fence around the yard). A second point: 넘다 ('go over') takes the object marker 을/를, so it's 담장을 넘다, not 담장에 넘다.

Its modern functional successor is 거실 (居室), the apartment living room: people in apartments overwhelmingly say 거실, while 마루 evokes an older hanok-style home, so describing your modern flat you'd say 거실에서 TV 봐요, not 마루에서. Because people sit and lie directly on it, 마루 pairs naturally with 앉다, 눕다, 시원하다, and 닦다. The English-speaker pitfall is the particle with 앉다: the spot where you sit takes 에 (마루에 앉아요), not 에서 — 에서 is for a broader activity (마루에서 쉬어요), but the precise location of sitting/lying is 에. 에 + 걸리다 (get caught); the spot you snag your foot
이/가 + 높다; literally and also figuratively 'hard to access'
을/를 + 조심하다; a common spoken warning
examples: 문턱이 좀 높아요.
The threshold is a bit high.
Simple description: 이 + adjective 높다

Everyday: 에 + 걸리다 + 을 뻔하다 (almost did)

That shop feels hard to walk into — the bar feels high.
Real-life idiom: 문턱이 높다 figuratively = intimidating / hard to access
nuance: 문턱 is the small raised step or sill at the bottom of a doorway that you step over when passing through. It's a native compound: 문 ('door') + 턱 ('ledge/step'), so it literally means 'the door's ledge.' Don't confuse it with the whole 문 (the door itself) or with 문지방 (a close synonym: the structural doorsill beam — 문지방 is the carpentry member, 문턱 the everyday word for the step you feel underfoot, and in daily speech 문턱 is far more common). Because it's a classic spot to stub a toe, it pairs with warnings (조심하다, 걸리다, 넘어지다). It also has a vivid idiom: 문턱이 높다 means figuratively 'the barrier to entry is high / it feels intimidating to go in' (그 회사는 문턱이 높다), and 문턱이 닳도록 드나들다 means 'visit so often you wear the doorsill down.' The English-speaker pitfall is the particle with 넘다: the sill is a direct object, so it's 문턱을 넘다, not 문턱에 넘다 — but 'trip ON it' uses 에 with 걸리다 (문턱에 걸리다). A second pitfall is taking 문턱이 높다 literally when a Korean means it figuratively.
